title: Automated Credentialing: How AI changes everything
summary: Go read how AI is redefining automated healthcare credentialing and how you can cut processing time from 60-120 days to under 30 days.
body_markdown:
If you are researching automated credentialing, your team is probably entering the same provider data into several systems, chasing missing documents, and checking portals for updates.


I know that administrative burden all too well.


Healthcare and provider credentialing work still happens in websites that do not have a suitable API and forces manual credentialing processes with time consuming manual data entry.


Someone still has to copy/paste data into a state board portal, CAQH, NPPES, or a payer portal.


I built Skyvern exactly to fix that (I am Skyvern’s CEO).


Skyvern automates that browser work with a mix of AI and computer vision to turn manual credentialing workflows into robust, repeatable and automated credentialing systems.


It gracefully handles attestations, disclosures, and decisions that require human judgment and asks for review when an answer is unclear, and records what happened.


Here is my take on what good credentialing automation is and how to get started.


## What credentialing actually means


Healthcare Credentialing is a general term for several connected processes:


- State medical licensing boards allowing clinicians to practice in a jurisdiction with the proper certifications
- CAQH ProView storing provider information that authorized healthcare organizations can access.
- NPPES assigning and maintaining National Provider Identifiers.
- Payers and healthcare organizations running their own enrollment, background checks, license verification, and privileging processes.


These systems use much of the same information, but they have different rules and purposes.


### Now for the automation part


[Healthcare credentialing automation](https://www.skyvern.com/healthcare?ref=skyvern.com) replaces manual verification of provider qualifications with software-driven workflows. Instead of staff manually entering data into state medical boards, CAQH ProView, and NPPES. Automated credentialing covers data validation, form entry, document uploads, status checks, renewals, and audit records. It moves approved provider data from an internal system into the correct portal.


Credentialing platforms and credentialing software’s purpose is to reduce repetitive administration.


Credentialing specialists still handle exceptions, verify information, and make decisions.


For example, when a new provider joins a group, the same approved record can be used for a state license application, a CAQH profile update, an NPI change, and later payer enrollment.


Each destination receives the fields and documents it requires. The specialist reviews conflicts instead of entering the same education, address, and license history four times.


## Why It Matters


The business case for automation is clear.


Traditional credentialing takes 60-120 days to complete, delaying revenue and straining administrative teams. The[U.S. credentialing software and services market](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/21/3192691/0/en/U-S-Credentialing-Software-and-Services-in-Healthcare-Market-Trends-Analysis-Report-2025-2033-Growth-Opportunities-Through-Automation-Enhancing-Regulatory-Compliance-and-Boosting-E.html?ref=skyvern.com) reached $267.72 million in 2024 and is growing at 6.95% annually through 2033.


Manual credentialing creates a lot of financial burden.[Physicians spend $7,618 annually](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/credentialing-software-services-healthcare-market-report?ref=skyvern.com) submitting applications to payers, before accounting for internal staff costs. Direct expenses include application fees, background checks, and salaries for credentialing specialists who spend weeks copying data between systems. A single credentialing coordinator costs $45,000-$65,000 yearly but processes only 15-20 applications monthly.


Credentialing touches every provider hire, contract renewal, and facility expansion. Each delayed credential means lost appointments and frustrated patients. Organizations handling dozens or hundreds of providers need automation to scale without proportionally increasing headcount.


## Why credentialing automation is difficult


The real challenge is keeping provider data consistent across health systems that were built independently, and for different purposes.


A legal name, practice address, taxonomy code, or work history may appear and be stored differently from one portal to another.


For example, each state board has its own requirements with different fields. Each asks different questions. Some other forms contain conditional questions.


On top of that, sessions expire, upload limits vary, multifactor authentication can interrupt the workflow.


Traditional credentialing applications and automation tools depend on fixed selectors and page paths, so even a small portal update can break them.


This is where AI browser automation is miles ahead (and where Skyvern shines!): it reads labels, page content, and surrounding context, so it can adapt to changes and achieve.


It still needs monitoring and a safe way to stop when the page or request falls outside the workflow’s rules, but it handles re-credentialing workflows, exclusions monitoring and compliance monitoring much better than the traditional automated credentialing platforms.


## Automating state medical board applications


State licensure is well… messy!


This is the least uniform part of credentialing.


Requirements, fees, forms, and verification processes vary by jurisdiction. Services such as the Federation of State Medical Boards’ Uniform Application and FCVS reduce some duplicate work, but they do not remove state-specific requirements.


This is where automated credentialing has the biggest impact in terms of saved time and cost saving.


And this is the exact scenario we built Skyvern for: navigating the complex mazes of manual data entry without constantly having an automation that breaks and add credentialing delays and stress on the credentialing team.


## Automating CAQH ProView


CAQH lets a provider maintain one profile and authorize participating organizations to access it. The profile still needs regular attention because licenses, insurance, addresses, and other details change.


Providers generally need to do re-credentialing every 120 days.


In this scenario, a good automation can compare the internal provider record with CAQH, prepare changes, upload current documents, and flag conflicts.


It can also track the next attestation date and notify the provider when review is required.


It still needs human oversight and verification to complete the final attestation under the organization’s policy.


The automation can prepare the profile, but it should not certify the accuracy of the information on someone else’s behalf.


## Automating NPPES and NPI updates


NPPES assigns and maintains the 10-digit National Provider Identifier used in standard healthcare transactions. Type 1 NPIs identify individuals, while Type 2 NPIs identify organizations.


An NPI does not prove that a provider is licensed, credentialed, or enrolled with a payer.[CMS makes that distinction clear](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/npi-fact-sheet.pdf?ref=skyvern.com) .


NPPES provides public lookup data through the NPI Registry, downloadable files, and an API. It also supports some bulk processes. Applications and updates may still require the NPPES portal or another CMS submission method.


Automation can prepare NPI applications, validate taxonomy codes, update addresses and authorized officials, compare internal records with public NPPES data, and save submission details.[Covered providers must report changes within 30 days](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/npi-fact-sheet.pdf?ref=skyvern.com) , so an update to the internal provider record should trigger the corresponding NPPES workflow.


NPPES updates do not automatically update Medicare enrollment or payer records. After a change is accepted, the workflow should identify the other systems that need the same correction. This prevents the internal record, NPPES, PECOS, CAQH, and payer portals from drifting apart.


## Automating exclusions monitoring and expiration tracking


Credentialing continues after a provider is approved!


State licenses, controlled substance registrations, board certifications, liability policies, and CAQH attestations can have expiration or reattestation dates.


A good automation can read those dates from the provider record, create renewal tasks based on the organization’s lead times, and alert the owner when required information is missing.


Exclusion monitoring requires a separate workflow. On the organization’s chosen schedule, the system should compare its active provider roster with the exclusion sources required by its policy.


For OIG screening, use the official List of Excluded Individuals and Entities and follow \[OIG’s verification instructions\]([https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/leie-quick-tips-instructions/](https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/leie-quick-tips-instructions/?ref=skyvern.com) ). The downloadable LEIE data is updated monthly.


A name match should go to a reviewer rather than trigger an automatic decision as common names and limited identifiers can produce false matches.

Your internal system is the primary source of data, your credentialing team defines the rules and handles exceptions and providers or authorized officials complete required attestations.


## Where to start


I recommend starting with one frequent workflow that has clear rules and clean inputs. A recurring CAQH document update, board status check, or standard NPPES address change is easier to evaluate than a rare license application with several disclosures.


Run the first version with human review before submission. Compare the proposed entries with what an experienced credentialing specialist would enter. Record every intervention, then turn repeated interventions into validation rules or defined approval steps.


Measure the completion rate, correction rate, time per provider, and share of runs that need review. Once the workflow is predictable, automate the low-risk steps and expand to another portal or provider type.


That is the balance we aim for at Skyvern: automate the work that software can perform reliably, and keep people in control of the decisions.
